'''''Tamarix ramosissima''''', commonly known as '''saltcedar'''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.html?sub=6515|title=saltcedar|publisher=Invasive Plant Atlas|access-date=April 24, 2019}}</ref> '''salt cedar''', or '''tamarisk''', is a [[deciduous]] arching shrub with reddish stems, feathery, pale green foliage, and characteristic small pink flowers.

The [[cultivar]] 'Pink Cascade' (dark pink flowered) has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHS">{{cite web |title=''Tamarix ramosissima'' 'Pink Cascade' {{!}} /RHS Gardening |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/47174/i-Tamarix-ramosissima-i-Pink-Cascade/Details |website=www.rhs.org.uk |access-date=31 May 2021 |language=en-gb}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=''Tamarix ramosissima'' 'Pink Cascade' |url=https://www.gardenersworld.com/plants/tamarix-ramosissima-pink-cascade/ |website=BBC Gardeners' World Magazine |access-date=31 May 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Tamarix ramossissima.jpg|thumb|Tamarix ramossissima at Villeurbanne, France]]
''Tamarix ramosissima'' is a hardy shrub or small tree native to Europe and Asia. It is a vigorous, deciduous shrub grown for its ornamental reddish stems, its showy plumes of flowers, and its unusual feathery leaves. Its hardiness and tolerance for poor soil make it a popular, easy to grow shrub. It can grow up to {{convert|8|m}} in height and up to {{convert|5|m}} in width. It can be used as a screen, windbreak, informal hedge or specimen shrub.<ref name=feis>Zouhar, Kris. 2003. [http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/tamspp/all.html ''Tamarix'' spp.] In: Fire Effects Information System, [Online]. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory.</ref>

It produces upright [[raceme]]s of small, pink, five-petaled flowers from late summer to early autumn which cover the new wood of the plant. It is tolerant of many soil types, but prefers a well-drained, light or sandy soil in full sun. This plant is considered an invasive species in warmer climates.<ref name=feis/>

This tamarisk [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridizes]] commonly with ''T.'' ''chinensis'' in the North American invasion<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gaskin |first=John F. |last2=Schaal |first2=Barbara A. |date=2002-08-20 |title=Hybrid Tamarix widespread in U.S. invasion and undetected in native Asian range |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.132403299 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=99 |issue=17 |pages=11256–11259 |doi=10.1073/pnas.132403299 |pmc=123243 |pmid=12177412}}</ref>.

==Invasive species==
''Tamarix ramosissima'' is a major [[Invasive species|invasive plant species]] in the [[Southwestern United States]] and [[Desert Region of California]], consuming large amounts of groundwater in [[riparian]] and [[oases]] [[habitats]].<ref name=feis/> The balance and strength of the native flora and fauna are being helped by various restoration projects, by removing tamarisk groves as if they were [[noxious weed]]s.<ref>[http://www.blm.gov/ca/st/en/fo/barstow/sltcdr97pa1.html Afton Canyon Riparian Restoration Project Fourth Year Status Report.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151206191327/http://www.blm.gov/ca/st/en/fo/barstow/sltcdr97pa1.html |date=2015-12-06 }} Bureau of Land Management. accessed 6/20/2010</ref> Recent scientific investigations have generally concluded that the primary human-caused impact to desert riparian ecosystems within the [[Colorado River#Watershed|Colorado River Basin]] is the alteration of the flood regime by dams; ''Tamarix ramosissima'' is relatively tolerant of this hydrologic alteration compared to flood-dependent native woody riparian species such as [[willow]], [[Populus|cottonwood]], and [[box elder]].<ref name=Wolf2016>{{cite web |author=Wolf, E. |date=June 6, 2016 |url=https://cwseducation.ucdavis.edu/class/106/science-driving-new-management-strategy-tamarix|title=Science driving a new management strategy for ''Tamarix''}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Shifting dominance of riparian Populus and Tamarix along gradients of flow alteration in western North American rivers|author1=David Merritt|author2=LeRoy Poff|journal=Ecological Applications|volume=20|pages=135-152|year=2010|url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/08-2251.1}}</ref>

Research on competition between tamarisk seedlings and co-occurring native trees has found that ''Tamarix'' seedlings are not competitive over a range of environments,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sher |first1=Anna A.|author1-link=Anna Sher |last2=Marshall |first2=Diane L. |last3=Gilbert |first3=Steven A. |year=2000 |title=Competition between native Populus deltoides and invasive Tamarix ramosissima and the implications of reestablishing flooding disturbance |journal=Conservation Biology |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=1744–1754 |doi=10.1046/j.1523-1739.2000.99306.x}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sher |first1=A.A. |last2=Marshall |first2=D.L. |last3=Taylor |first3=J.P. |date=June 2002 |title=Establishment patterns of native ''Populus'' and ''Salix'' in the presence of invasive, non-native ''Tamarix'' |journal=Ecological Applications |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=760–772 |doi=10.1890/1051-0761(2002)012[0760:eponpa]2.0.co;2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sher |title=Competition between native and exotic floodplain tree species across water regimes and soil textures |journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=90| year=2003| pages=413–422 |doi=10.3732/ajb.90.3.413 |pmid=21659134 |first1=A. A. |last2=Marshall |first2=D. L. |issue=3| doi-access=free}}</ref> but stands of mature trees effectively prevent native species' establishment in the [[understory]], due to low light, elevated salinity, and possibly changes to the [[soil biota]].<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Mechanisms associated with decline of woody species in riparian ecosystems of the southwestern U.S |journal=Ecological Monographs |volume=65| year=1995| pages=347–370 |doi=10.2307/2937064 |author1=Busch, David E. |author2=Smith, Stanley D. |issue=3 |jstor=2937064}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Taylor |first1=J. |last2=McDaniel |first2=K. |title=Restoration of saltcedar (Tamarix spp.)-infested floodplains on the Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge |journal=Weed Technology |date=1998 |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=345–352 |doi= 10.1017/S0890037X0004392X}}</ref> Box elder (''[[Acer negundo]]'', a native riparian tree) seedlings survive and grow under higher-shade conditions than ''Tamarix'' seedlings, and mature ''Tamarix'' specimens die after 1–2 years of 98% shade, indicating a pathway for successional replacement of ''Tamarix'' by box elder.<ref>{{Cite journal| last1=Dewine| first1=J. ==Salt==
The plant's common name refers to its ability to tolerate [[salt water]]<ref name="Which came first">[http://www.coloradoriparian.org/which-came-first-the-salt-or-the-saltcedar/ Which came first, the salt or the saltcedar? A quantitative study of soil and groundwater chemistry along the Middle Rio Grande, New Mexico], by Michelle Cederborg, at the Colorado Riparian Association; published April 20, 2008; retrieved April 24, 2019</ref> by excreting salt into its leaves through specialized salt glands — thereby producing salt deposits which kill other species;<ref name=TontoNationalForest>[http://www.fs.usda.gov/r03/tonto Invasive Weeds - Salt Cedar], at the USDA Forest Service; retrieved April 24, 2019</ref> these salt deposits can also weaken interatomic binding in soil clays, leading to increased erosion.<ref name="Which came first"/> However, a study involving more than a thousand soil samples across gradients of both flood frequency and ''Tamarix'' density concluded that "flooding may be the most important factor for assessing floodplain salinity" and "soils under ''Tamarix'' canopies had lower surface soil salinity than open areas deprived of flooding suggesting that surface evaporation may contribute more to surface soil salinity than ''Tamarix''".<ref name=Ohrtman2009>{{cite web |author=Ohrtman, M. |date=2009 |url=http://digitalcommons.du.edu/etd/485/ |title=Quantifying soil and groundwater chemistry in areas invaded by ''Tamarix'' spp. along the Middle Rio Grande, New Mexico}}</ref>
